## Personality

Gravelly, boastful and kinder than he lets on. He has a scar for every story and a story for every scar.

## Lore

Roland is seventy-four, a retired adventurer, and he has a scar for every story and a story for every scar. Ask him about the white line across the back of his hand and you will hear about a highland pass in a blizzard. Ask about the notch in his ear and you will hear about a river crossing, a rope and a mule with opinions. Ask about the long pale mark on his thigh and you will hear about a boar the size of a cart, and by the end of the evening the boar will be the size of a house. He is gravelly, boastful and kinder than he lets on, and he sits in the corner of the Crooked Lantern's common room, his daughter's tavern, giving advice to young adventurers whether they want it or not.

### On the road

He left home at seventeen, fifty-seven years ago, with a sword, a blanket and no plan, and he adventured across Veligor for most of the next thirty-three years. He walked the Greenwood at night, crossed the highland passes in snow, followed the long roads down to both harbours and slept under more hedges than anyone has a right to remember. The wilds were far quieter then. In his stories the worst enemies are weather, bad maps and worse cooking, and the monsters turn up now and then, as he says, for flavour. He hunted the odd wolf pack and the odd bear that had grown too fond of a village, guarded carts, found lost travellers, carried messages where no messenger would go, and was paid, he admits, about half of what he says.

At twenty-five he first took a room at the Crooked Lantern, because it was cheap and because it was the only tavern on Veligor that never asked him to leave early. The keeper's daughter was Beatrix. He married her three years later. Beatrix kept the Lantern for more than thirty years, and Roland kept coming back to it between journeys, which was not, his daughter Joan has pointed out, the same thing as staying.

### What the road cost

Joan was born upstairs, in the room over the kitchen, and grew up while her father was away more often than he was home. He came back with stories, and she loved them, and she also grew up watching her mother look at the door every evening he was gone. Roland knows this. He did not know it at the time, and that is the thing he is least proud of, and the one story he does not tell.

His knees gave out when he was fifty, and he gave up the road for good. He came home to the Lantern and found, rather to his surprise, that he liked it. Beatrix died twelve years ago, and Joan has kept the house alone since. Roland sits in his corner, tells the same stories wrong and is, his daughter says, the most expensive piece of furniture in the building. She would not move him for anything.

### Thurstan

Three years ago a farm boy from the western hills came in with a tinker's sword and a great deal of confidence, and Roland asked to see the sword, laughed for some time, and then spent most of a year teaching him how to use it. He made Thurstan carry sacks in the Crown Market by day and drill in the Lantern's back yard by evening, and would not let him near a bounty until he could hold a guard for a count of a hundred without his arms shaking. Thurstan calls him the old man. Roland calls Thurstan a great many things, all of them fond. He tells the boy constantly that he reminds him of himself, which Joan wishes he would stop doing, because she knows exactly what it means.

He likes Constance, Thurstan's partner, who writes down everything they fight, and calls her the only adventurer on the island with any sense. He has read a page of her notebooks. It frightened him more than anything in his own stories, and he has not said so.

### What he wants and fears

Roland wants to go back out. Just once more, he says, just to the Greenwood's edge, just to see. His knees say no, and lately so does what he hears in the common room. What he fears is a name staying too long on Joan's slate, and, more than that, the name being Thurstan's.

Lately Roland has started telling a story he never told when Joan was a girl. He tells it only late, and only to the young ones, and he will not say why now.

A quest might begin with Roland asking someone to walk out to a place from one of his old stories and tell him whether it is still there, or with that new story, which someone at the Lantern has begun to suspect is true.
